summary: Project Astravitalis is Nabd, a crew health-monitoring and decision-support web app for long-duration space missions. On a Mars mission, a message to a flight surgeon can take up to 22 minutes each way, so astronauts must assess their own health. Nabd gathers a 2-minute daily check-in (camera-based pulse, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, nutrition, training and a reaction-time test) and maps every result to NASA's five spaceflight hazards on an interactive body map. A rules engine compares each astronaut with their own baseline, gives a green, amber or red status with plain-language reasons, and recommends specific actions. Mission modes (space station, Mars transit, lunar base) change hazards, gravity, radiation and communication delay, with offline-first behavior and structured reports for the flight surgeon. Scenarios such as a solar storm show how risks develop over time. Nabd is decision support, not diagnosis, and all mission data in the demo is simulated.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Nabd helps astronauts evaluate and act on their own health when Earth cannot help in real time. A 2-minute daily check-in collects pulse (including a camera-based reading processed in the browser), blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, hydration, nutrition, exercise and a short reaction-time test. An interactive body map shows the status of each system (heart, brain, bones, muscles, metabolism, immune system, mind). Selecting a zone explains its function, why spaceflight affects it, which NASA hazard is responsible, and what to do next.

HOW IT WORKS

A transparent rules engine compares every value with the individual's own baseline and approximate reference ranges, then returns green (continue), amber (self-care actions) or red (contact the flight surgeon) with a plain-language reason. Trend detection highlights slow drift before a threshold is crossed. Mission modes (space station, Mars transit, lunar base) change radiation rates, gravity and communication delay. In Mars mode, reports to the flight surgeon show delivery states while an "autonomous decision window" lists safe actions to take while waiting. Scenarios such as a solar storm, CO2 rise and isolation drift show how hazards affect indicators over time.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Long missions will place crews far from hospitals. Nabd lets them notice problems early, understand them, and escalate with a structured report. The same approach applies on Earth to Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics, where help is delayed and bandwidth is limited.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Personal-baseline early warning instead of fixed thresholds; every status explained and linked to a NASA hazard; mission modes with communication delay; a beginner-friendly design that explains how and why each measurement is taken.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, Framer Motion, Supabase (database, storage, realtime), browser-based camera pulse estimation (vitallens.js), jsPDF for reports. [EDIT: list only what your app actually uses.]

NASA AND PARTNER RESOURCES

Hazard-to-indicator mapping and educational text are based on NASA Human Research Program pages on hazards, risks and ongoing research. The radiation indicator is informed by Canadian Space Agency material. Reference ranges and radiation rates are approximate public figures and are labelled as such in the app.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

We used SI tools as follows: Lovable (AI app builder) generated much of the application code; built-in AI provides in-app explanations, daily plans and photo-scan observations; image generation produced crew avatars, backgrounds and icons, each carrying a visible "AI-generated" watermark; Claude (Anthropic) assisted with planning, prompts, slide text and documentation. Our team defined the concept and requirements, chose the science sources, tested the app and reviewed all content.

LIMITATIONS

Nabd is decision support, not a medical device, and gives no diagnoses, drug names or doses. Camera pulse accuracy depends on lighting and motion. All mission data in the demo is simulated; no real astronaut data was used.
